title: Prompting vs RAG vs long context vs fine-tuning
summary: Prompting and context carry facts at run time, RAG fetches them per question, long context preloads them, and fine-tuning changes behaviour. Evidence says use fine-tuning for style, not for facts.
useIf: You decide how a model gets knowledge or a behaviour it does not have.
avoidIf: You pick a method before measuring corpus size, update rate, permissions, volume and accuracy needs.

explain.md: Separate two needs. **Knowledge** (facts the model lacks) belongs in the context, supplied by a prompt, a preloaded long context or retrieval. **Behaviour** (format, tone, tool use, a smaller model) can be learned by fine-tuning. OpenAI lists fine-tuning benefits as format, shorter prompts, smaller models and private data [[r48]], and Azure says fine-tuning does not replace retrieval for current information [[r17]].

**Cache-augmented generation (CAG)** preloads documents into a long context and caches the runtime state, so there is no retrieval step. The paper says it suits a limited, manageable knowledge base [[r24]]. Anthropic says a knowledge base under about 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages, an estimate) can go straight into the prompt, and prompt caching makes that cheaper and faster [[r42]]. Past that, or when access differs by user, retrieval wins.

explain.title: How should the model get this knowledge?
explain.prompt: Flip the dials. The ranking and the reasons update.

options.name: Long context plus caching (CAG)
options.summary: Preload the documents and cache the prefix.

options.name: RAG
options.summary: Retrieve the relevant chunks per question.

small.why: Fits the window and needs no retrieval stack.

large.why: Exceeds the window or degrades deep in context.

user.why: A shared prefix cannot hold per-user content.

small.why: Works, with more moving parts than needed.
New facts are learned slowly and can raise hallucination.

large.why: Weights cannot reliably hold a large corpus.

stable.why: Still weaker than retrieval for facts.

fast.why: Retraining for each change is impractical.

explain.takeaway: Fine-tuning scores low here because this board is about knowledge. It wins when the goal is format, tone, tool use or a smaller model. Combine RAG with a tuned model when you need both facts and style.

explain.md: Evidence behind the dials: Chroma tested 18 LLMs and found performance grows unreliable as input grows [[r22]]. RULER found only about half of models claiming 32K or more stayed satisfactory at 32K [[r23]], and in NoLiMa 11 of 13 models fell below 50% of their short-context baseline at 32K [[r41]]. RAG consistently beat unsupervised fine-tuning for knowledge [[r43]], and new facts learned by fine-tuning raise hallucination [[r44]].

whereToUse: Internal handbooks and policy sets: long context when small, RAG when large or permissioned
Product and support knowledge that changes weekly: RAG with incremental indexing
Brand voice, report formats and tool-use habits: fine-tuning or few-shot prompting
Cost control at volume: fine-tune a smaller model to replace a long prompt
Interview answers about grounding an assistant, using the dials above

use: Long context plus caching when the corpus is small, stable and one audience
RAG when the corpus is large, changes often or access differs by user
Fine-tuning when you need behaviour or format and have examples
Hybrid when you need current facts and a consistent style
avoid: Stuffing a large corpus into a prompt because the window allows it
RAG for a 50-page stable handbook that fits in a cached prompt
flips: Corpus outgrows about 200,000 tokens, or accuracy drops deep in context: move to RAG
Permissions become per user: choose retrieval with access filters
A long few-shot prompt costs too much at volume: consider fine-tuning a smaller model, if the platform allows

pitfalls.symptom: The assistant answers confidently from outdated facts after fine-tuning
pitfalls.cause: Facts were trained into weights and the source changed
pitfalls.fix: Move facts to retrieval and keep fine-tuning for behaviour

pitfalls.symptom: Answers miss facts placed deep in a very long prompt
pitfalls.cause: Accuracy falls as input grows and with position in the context
pitfalls.fix: Test with answers at different depths, shorten the context or use retrieval

pitfalls.symptom: A shared cached prompt exposes content to the wrong users
pitfalls.cause: Per-user content was put into a shared prefix
pitfalls.fix: Keep per-user content out of shared prefixes and use filtered retrieval

scenarios.title: Large, fast-changing, permissioned knowledge
scenarios.situation: An assistant answers from several million tokens of documents that change hourly. Each employee may see only some documents, and answers need citations.
unknowns: How fast must a revocation apply?
What accuracy is expected on exact identifiers?
scenarios.question: How does the model get the knowledge?

options.name: Fine-tune a model on the documents weekly
options.why: Facts go stale between runs, weights cannot enforce per-user access and there are no citations.
options.tradeoff: Fine-tuning is right for style or format on stable examples.

options.name: Long context with a cached prefix of the most-used documents
options.tradeoff: It cannot hold the corpus or enforce per-user access in a shared prefix.

options.name: RAG with incremental indexing and per-user security filters
options.why: Handles size, hourly changes, permissions and citations together.
options.tradeoff: You build and tune ingestion, retrieval and access control.

flips.then: Add a live permission check on hits.

flips.if: Only a small slice is needed and is public
flips.then: A cached prompt for that slice is simpler.

scenarios.takeaway: Size, churn and permissions point to retrieval.

scenarios.title: A 150,000 token handbook with a tight latency target
scenarios.situation: A team builds an HR helper over a single 150,000 token handbook. It changes quarterly, has one audience and needs answers within 3 seconds at p95.
unknowns: Does accuracy hold at the deepest handbook positions?
How many questions share the prefix?
scenarios.question: Which approach do you start with?

options.name: Preload the handbook and cache the prefix
options.why: It fits the roughly 200,000 token guidance, skips retrieval and keeps latency low [[r42]] [[r24]].
options.tradeoff: Test accuracy at different depths, and expect the cache to reset on each quarterly update.

options.name: RAG with hybrid search and a reranker
options.tradeoff: Adds ingestion, an index and tuning the constraints do not need.

options.name: Fine-tune a model on the handbook
options.why: Facts are learned slowly, can raise hallucination and give no citations.

flips.if: The handbook grows well past the window

scenarios.takeaway: Small and stable favours the simplest option that works.

scenarios.title: A 6,000 token prompt run two million times a month
scenarios.situation: A support tool needs a strict five-section reply in a brand voice. A prompt with 20 examples works but costs too much at two million requests a month. The team has 2,000 approved replies and runs on Azure OpenAI.
constraints: Behaviour and format, not new facts
unknowns: Does a smaller tuned model match the prompt baseline?
When does the base model retire?
scenarios.question: What do you try?

options.name: Keep the long few-shot prompt and rely on prompt caching
options.why: No training and quick to run.
options.tradeoff: Pays for the cached prefix each call and relies on cache hits.

options.name: Fine-tune a smaller supported model with SFT on the approved replies, compare it with the prompt baseline, and check its retirement date
options.why: The need is format and tone with data in hand, and a shorter prompt cuts cost at volume.
options.tradeoff: Training effort, a retirement date to track, and re-tuning if the style changes.

options.name: Use RAG over past replies to teach the tone
options.why: Retrieval supplies facts and examples per query. It is a weak way to enforce a consistent format.
options.tradeoff: RAG fits when the examples are knowledge, such as past answers to specific cases.

flips.if: The platform is OpenAI directly and the org has no fine-tuning history
flips.then: New fine-tuning jobs may be blocked, so use prompting or Azure.
Prompting is cheaper than repeated tuning.

scenarios.takeaway: Tune for behaviour at volume, and verify the platform still offers it.

quiz.q: Which approach does the evidence favour for adding new facts to a model?
options: Retrieval or context supplied at run time
quiz.explain: Ovadia et al. found RAG consistently beat unsupervised fine-tuning, and Gekhman et al. found new facts learned through fine-tuning raise hallucination.

quiz.q: Which dial changes push you from a cached long prompt to RAG?
quiz.explain: Size, per-user access and frequent change all break a shared cached prefix. A preference for short prompts does not change the answer.

quiz.q: Match each approach to its best-fit job.

pairs.r: Large, changing or permissioned corpus with citations
Moving a large model's behaviour to a small model

quiz.explain: Each approach has a primary job. Mixing them up leads to fine-tuning for facts or RAG for tone.

flashcards.back: Behaviour: format, tone, tool use, shorter prompts and smaller models. It is weak for adding facts.

flashcards.front: What is CAG and when does it fit?
flashcards.back: Cache-augmented generation preloads documents and caches runtime state. It fits a small, stable corpus, roughly under 200,000 tokens per Anthropic's guidance.

flashcards.front: Name three studies behind the long-context caution.
flashcards.back: Chroma Context Rot (18 LLMs), RULER (17 models) and NoLiMa (13 models, 11 below 50% of baseline at 32K).
